nameStory: The Purple Tiger Beetle gets its name from the stunning metallic purple sheen that flashes across its wing covers when sunlight hits them just right. Like all tiger beetles, it earned the "tiger" part of its name from its fierce hunting style — these beetles are aggressive predators that chase down prey with lightning speed, much like a big cat stalking through the forest.
description: The Purple Tiger Beetle is a dazzling metallic beetle about half an inch long that looks like a tiny jewel scurrying across sandy paths and open ground. Its body gleams with rich purple, violet, and sometimes greenish metallic colors that shift and shimmer as it moves. These speedy hunters have large, prominent eyes and powerful legs built for quick sprints. You'll often see them darting ahead of you on trails, stopping suddenly, then zooming off again in their characteristic stop-and-go fashion.

idTips.label: Metallic purple coloration
idTips.description: Wing covers shine with deep purple to violet metallic colors that change intensity in different light angles, sometimes showing hints of green or copper

idTips.label: Large bulging eyes
idTips.description: Prominent, forward-facing eyes that stick out noticeably from the head, giving excellent vision for hunting

idTips.label: Lightning-fast movement
idTips.description: Runs in quick bursts with sudden stops, often staying just ahead of approaching footsteps on paths

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a streamlined, athletic body shape and long, powerful legs built for speed

idTips.label: Mandibles
idTips.description: Large, curved jaws that project forward from the head, visible even from a distance

habitat: Purple Tiger Beetles love sandy or packed dirt paths, especially cow paths and hiking trails where the soil stays firm and relatively bare. You'll find them in open woodlands, field edges, and along dirt roads where there's good sun exposure and loose, well-drained soil. They prefer areas with some vegetation nearby but need clear, open ground for hunting their prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active on warm, sunny days, often seen running along trails and open patches where the ground has warmed up.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and easiest to spot, actively hunting during the warmest part of sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall on warm days, though they become less common as temperatures drop and may seek shelter.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden under logs, rocks, or buried in soil, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Purple Tiger Beetles are so fast they actually run blind — they sprint so quickly (up to 5 mph, which is blazingly fast for their tiny size) that their eyes can't process images fast enough, so they have to stop periodically to relocate their prey and figure out where they're going!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other metallic tiger beetles, especially the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle, but the Purple Tiger Beetle lacks the distinctive white spots and has that rich purple coloration instead of bright green. Memory trick: "Purple" in the name matches the "purple" you see — if it's green with white spots, it's the Six-spotted instead.
contextualKnowledge: The alternate name "Cow Path Tiger Beetle" reflects this species' love of packed dirt trails created by livestock, though you'll find them on any similar packed-earth path including hiking trails and dirt roads.
compareHints: Unlike the bright metallic green Six-spotted Tiger Beetle with its obvious white spots, the Purple Tiger Beetle shows deep purple metallic colors without distinct white markings. It's also generally smaller and more slender than the robust Bronzed Tiger Beetle, and lacks the distinctive banding patterns seen in species like the Twelve-spotted Tiger Beetle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tiger beetles, the six-spotted stands out for its pure metallic green color - the bronzed tiger beetle has more copper tones, while the festive tiger beetle is darker with different spot patterns.

Among New England's tiger beetles, the Bronzed Tiger Beetle is distinguished by its warm copper-bronze coloration, while the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle shines bright metallic green and the Purple Tiger Beetle displays cooler purple-blue tones.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the festive tiger beetle is distinguished by its particular pattern of white markings and metallic coloration.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Hairy-necked is the only one with those distinctive fuzzy neck hairs.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the twelve-spotted is unique for having exactly twelve spots on a dark body.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Oblique-lined stands out with its exceptionally large compound eyes and distinctive diagonal white markings.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Big Sand Tiger Beetle stands out for its robust, chunky build compared to the more slender Six-spotted or Bronzed Tiger Beetles.

Unlike the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle which prefers woodland paths, or the Bronzed Tiger Beetle found on sandy beaches, the Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is the only New England tiger beetle that specializes in clay habitats.
